newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam dong slips as dollar demand keeps up.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam dong slips as dollar demand keeps up.

text.p: The Vietnamese dong slipped further towards the bottom of its new, wider trading band on Monday as demand for the U.S. currency continued apace, dealers said.
"There are some sellers (of dollars) entering the market, in smallish, modest amounts," said Peter McClean, Head of Treasury at Standard Chartered Bank in Hanoi.
"The market is finding a balance, but still at this point in time there are more buyers than sellers," he said.
The central bank's official rate was set at 11,088/99 per dollar on Tuesday compared with 11,055/85 on Saturday. The last interbank dealings quote was 11,099/110 per dollar.
Ten days ago the central State Bank of Vietnam widened the official fluctuation band for the dong to plus or minus 1.0 percent from plus or minus 0.5 percent.
The new band, like the previous one, has 11,030 per dollar as its pivot rate, with the upper end at 10,920 and the lower end at 11,140.

Bankers said the decision served to enliven a moribund market which had stalled near the bottom of the old band, 11,085, because of demand for the dollar which had built up ahead of the year-end and on rumours that the dong would be devalued.
The authorities have made it clear that a devaluation of the dong, although suggested by some as a solution to the country's widening trade gap, was not being planned.

The government-run weekly Vietnam Investment Review quoted Nguyen Doan Hung, head of the State Bank's forex department, as saying the band-widening move would allow commercial banks to set rates which reflect the true supply and demand picture.
"It is one of our efforts to improve the forex market," Hung was quoted as saying.
Dealers agreed that the wider band would deregulate the market and bring commercial banks' quotes closer to black market rates.
One dealer said the black market dong rate in Ho Chi Minh City was currently around 11,150 per dollar and in Hanoi it was around 11,180.
Bankers said that although devaluation has been ruled out, the widening of the trading bands has allowed the central bank to implement a policy of gradual depreciation.

The United Nations, in a report published last week, said trade liberalisation could provide an opportunity for "a gradual and orderly depreciation of the exchange rate to a more competitive level and better position Vietnam to compete" in international trade.
